mainEntity.name: Is Scottish income tax the same as the rest of the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. For 2026/27 Scotland uses six bands on non-savings, non-dividend income: starter 19%, basic 20%, intermediate 21%, higher 42%, advanced 45% and top 48%. England, Wales and Northern Ireland use 20%, 40% and 45%. National Insurance is the same across the UK.

mainEntity.name: Does National Insurance change in Scotland?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Employee Class 1 National Insurance is reserved to the UK. This page uses 0% up to £12,570, 8% to £50,270 and 2% above that — the same rates as the England, Wales and NI take-home calculator.

mainEntity.name: Which student loan plan should a Scottish employee pick?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most Scottish undergraduates are on Plan 4. The deduction is still the UK PAYE rule: 9% of monthly pay above the published Plan 4 threshold, rounded down to the nearest pound. Confirm the plan in your Student Finance account.

mainEntity.name: Who pays less tax, Scotland or the rest of the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: On employment income with a full personal allowance and no pension, a Scottish taxpayer pays less income tax than England, Wales and NI at £20,000 (by £39.67) and more at £35,000 (by £15.07) and at £60,000 (by £1,750.05). The crossover is inside the intermediate band. Dividends and savings interest stay on UK rates and are not in this comparison.

mainEntity.name: Is this exactly what PAYE will take this month?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. This is an annualised estimate on an S1257L-style full personal allowance. Real PAYE uses cumulative tables and per-period rounding, so a single month can differ by a few pounds.
